title: From Jesus to the Reformation and Beyond
bigQuestion: How did a small movement in Roman Judea become the world's largest religion, and why did it split into so many churches?

story.title: Two Letters from Two Jails
story.kicker: Almost two thousand years apart, two prisoners write letters that are read aloud to crowds.
paragraphs: Around 60 CE, a man named Paul sits in a rented house in Rome with a Roman soldier guarding him. The book of Acts says he stayed there two years, welcoming everyone who came. Paul was a Jewish teacher who had come to believe that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah. He wrote letters to small groups of believers in cities around the Mediterranean.

His letters were not read quietly by one person. They were read aloud when believers gathered, often in someone's home. In one letter, to the believers at Philippi, the writer says his chains have helped spread his message. Scholars debate where each letter was written. But Christians have read these letters aloud in worship ever since.

In April 1963, another prisoner sat in a jail cell in Birmingham, Alabama. He was Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister. He had been arrested for leading a peaceful march against segregation. Local clergy had called the protests unwise and untimely. King answered them in a long letter, written at first in the margins of a newspaper.

King's letter was soon printed and read aloud in churches and meetings across the country. He pointed to Paul, who carried his message from town to town. Between these two jails lie almost two thousand years of Christian history. This chapter follows that history from Judea to Chicago.
story.think: Why might a letter written from jail have special power when it is read aloud to a group?

lessons.title: Judea Under Rome
lessons.mainIdea: Jesus lived in Judea and Galilee while the Roman Empire ruled, a time when many Jews hoped for a Messiah.
reading: Roman coins from the first century show the face of the emperor. People in Judea paid taxes with coins like these. Rome had taken control of the region in 63 BCE. It ruled through local kings, such as Herod, and through Roman governors, such as Pontius Pilate, who governed from about 26 to 36 CE.

Many Jews at this time hoped for a *Messiah*, a word meaning anointed one. In Jewish tradition, the Messiah would be a leader from King David's family who would bring justice and peace. Jewish groups disagreed about how and when that would happen. Some waited and prayed. Some wanted to fight Rome.

Into this world, around 4 BCE, Jesus was born. He grew up in the village of Nazareth in Galilee. He was Jewish. He went to the synagogue, kept the festivals and taught from the Hebrew scriptures. Christians later came to believe that he was the Messiah. In Greek, Messiah is Christos, which gives us the word Christ.

words.d: anointed one; in Jewish tradition a hoped-for leader from David's family; Christians believe Jesus is the Messiah
from the Greek word for Messiah; a title Christians give to Jesus

look.title: A Coin in Your Hand
look.text: Picture a small silver coin. On one side is the Roman emperor's head. A Jewish farmer in Galilee must use it to pay a tax to a foreign empire. The farmer also prays three times a day to the God of Israel.
look.prompt: What might this farmer have hoped for? How does the coin help explain why many people longed for a Messiah?

check.q: What does the word Messiah mean?
check.why: Messiah means anointed one. Christ comes from the Greek word with the same meaning.

check.q: Which empire ruled Judea when Jesus lived?
check.why: Rome took control of Judea in 63 BCE and ruled there in Jesus' time.

check.q: Which statement about Jesus is accurate?
choices: He was Jewish and taught from the Hebrew scriptures
check.why: Jesus was Jewish. He kept the festivals and taught from the Hebrew scriptures.

lessons.title: Jesus in the Gospels
lessons.mainIdea: Four Gospels tell Jesus' story; Christians believe he died on a cross and rose from the dead.
reading: The *Gospels* are four books in the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Gospel means good news. They were written in Greek, most likely between c. 65 and 100 CE. Each tells Jesus' story in its own way. Christians read them aloud in worship every week.

The Gospels say Jesus taught in parables, short stories with a lesson. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, a stranger from a rival group helps a hurt traveler whom others walked past. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus blesses the poor, the grieving and the peacemakers. He tells his followers to love even their enemies.

The Gospels say that Jesus was crucified by Roman order in Jerusalem, around 30 CE. Christians believe that he rose from the dead three days later. This is called the *resurrection*. Christians celebrate it at Easter. Jews and Muslims honor Jesus in different ways, or not as Messiah, and do not share this belief about him.

words.d: good news; one of the four books that tell Jesus' life: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John
a short story with a lesson
rising from the dead; Christians believe Jesus rose three days after his death

look.title: From the Sermon on the Mount
look.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
look.prompt: Who is blessed in this line, and what is their reward? How might a listener try to live by it?

check.q: Which are the four Gospels?
check.why: The four Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.

check.q: What is a parable?
choices: A short story with a lesson
check.why: A parable is a short story with a lesson, like the Good Samaritan.

check.q: What do Christians celebrate at Easter?
check.why: Christians celebrate Jesus' resurrection at Easter. Christmas marks his birth.

lessons.title: Paul and the Early Church
lessons.mainIdea: Paul's travels and letters helped spread the faith to non-Jews across the Roman world.
reading: After Jesus' death, his followers kept meeting in Jerusalem. At first they were Jews who believed Jesus was the Messiah. The book of Acts tells how the message spread. A key figure was *Paul*, who had first opposed the believers. Acts says he changed after a vision of Jesus on the road to Damascus.

Paul traveled by road and by ship to cities like Corinth, Ephesus and Philippi. He taught that non-Jews, called Gentiles, could join without first becoming Jewish. His letters, called *epistles*, are the oldest writings in the New Testament. They date to c. 50 to 60 CE.

The early believers came to be called the *church*, from a Greek word for an assembly. They met in homes, shared a meal and baptized new members with water. Paul wrote that differences of people and status should not divide them. By 100 CE, small churches existed in many cities of the empire.

words.d: a letter; the letters of Paul and others in the New Testament
a community of Christians, from a Greek word for assembly; also the building where they meet
a person who is not Jewish

look.title: Paul to the Galatians
look.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
look.prompt: Name the three pairs Paul lists. What is he telling a mixed group of believers about how to treat one another?

check.q: What is an epistle?
check.why: An epistle is a letter, like Paul's letters in the New Testament.

check.q: What did Paul teach about Gentiles?
choices: They had to live in Jerusalem
They had to become Roman soldiers
They could join without first becoming Jewish
check.why: Paul taught that non-Jews could join the believers without first becoming Jewish.

check.q: Which writings are the oldest in the New Testament?
check.why: Paul's letters date to c. 50 to 60 CE, before the Gospels were written.

lessons.title: Martyrs, Constantine and the Creed
lessons.mainIdea: Christians were at times persecuted until Constantine allowed their faith in 313 CE; church councils then wrote creeds.
reading: In Rome, you can still walk through catacombs, underground burial tunnels. Early Christians painted pictures on the walls, such as a shepherd carrying a sheep. At times Roman rulers punished Christians for refusing to worship the emperor and the gods. Those who died for their faith are honored as *martyrs*.

Then things changed. In 312 CE, the general Constantine won a battle for control of Rome. He later said he had seen a sign of Christ before it. In 313 CE, Constantine and his co-emperor issued the Edict of Milan. It allowed Christians to worship freely. By 380 CE, a later emperor made Christianity the empire's official faith.

Christians disagreed about how to describe Jesus and God. In 325 CE, bishops met at Nicaea. They wrote a *creed*, a short statement of belief. The Nicene Creed says Christians believe in one God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This belief is called the Trinity. Many churches still say this creed every Sunday.

words.d: a person who dies rather than give up their faith
a short statement of belief, like the Nicene Creed
the Christian belief in one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit

look.title: The Opening of the Nicene Creed
look.text: We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things seen and unseen.
look.cite: Nicene Creed, Council of Nicaea 325 CE, expanded at Constantinople 381 CE; in our own words from common English versions
look.prompt: The creed starts with we believe. Why would a church want all its members to say the same words together?

check.q: What did the Edict of Milan do in 313 CE?
check.why: The Edict of Milan, in 313 CE, allowed Christians to worship freely.

check.q: What is a creed?
check.why: A creed is a short statement of belief, like the Nicene Creed.

check.q: What do Christians mean by the Trinity?
choices: One God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit
check.why: The Trinity is the Christian belief in one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

lessons.title: East, West and the Middle Ages
lessons.mainIdea: In 1054 the church split into Catholic and Orthodox, while monasteries, cathedrals and universities shaped medieval Europe.
reading: Over time, the church in the east, centered on Constantinople, and the church in the west, centered on Rome, grew apart. They spoke different languages, Greek and Latin. They disagreed about the power of the *pope*, the bishop of Rome. In 1054, leaders of the two sides excommunicated each other. This is often called the Great Schism.

Today the western church is the Roman Catholic Church, led by the pope. The eastern churches are the Eastern *Orthodox* churches, led by patriarchs and bishops. Orthodox worship uses icons, painted images of Christ and the saints. In 1965, a pope and a patriarch lifted the old excommunications.

In medieval Europe, *monasteries* were communities of monks or nuns who lived by a rule of prayer and work. Many followed the Rule of Saint Benedict, from c. 530 CE. Monks copied books by hand. Towns built great cathedrals. Church schools grew into the first universities, such as Bologna and Paris.

words.d: the bishop of Rome and leader of the Roman Catholic Church
in Christianity, the eastern churches, such as the Greek and Russian Orthodox churches
a community where monks or nuns live by a rule of prayer and work

look.title: Milestones in the Church's First Thousand Years
look.cite: Commonly given dates; Benedict's Rule is approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Edict of Milan and the split of 1054?

check.q: What happened in 1054?
choices: The church split into Catholic and Orthodox
check.why: In 1054 leaders of the eastern and western churches excommunicated each other.

check.q: Who leads the Roman Catholic Church?
check.why: The pope, the bishop of Rome, leads the Roman Catholic Church. Orthodox churches are led by patriarchs and bishops.

check.q: What is a monastery?
choices: A community of monks or nuns who pray and work
check.why: A monastery is a community where monks or nuns live by a rule of prayer and work.

lessons.title: Luther and the Printing Press
lessons.mainIdea: In 1517 Martin Luther challenged church practices, and the printing press spread his ideas fast, starting the Protestant Reformation.
reading: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg in Germany built a printing press with movable metal letters. Books that once took months to copy by hand could now be printed by the hundreds. Pamphlets could spread across a country in weeks. This new tool changed how ideas moved.

In 1517, a monk and teacher named Martin Luther wrote the *95 Theses*. They criticized the sale of indulgences, papers said to reduce punishment for sin. Luther taught that people are saved by God's grace through faith, not by buying anything. He also taught that the Bible was the highest authority. He translated the New Testament into German so ordinary people could read it.

Printers copied Luther's writings and spread them fast. The church leadership condemned his ideas, and he was excommunicated in 1521. His followers came to be called *Protestants*, from their protest. The movement is called the Reformation, an effort to reform, or change, the church.

words.d: the 1500s movement to reform the church, which led to Protestant churches
a Christian in one of the churches that grew from the Reformation
Luther's 1517 list of arguments against the sale of indulgences

look.title: Old Idea, New Tool
look.text: In 1517, Luther writes 95 arguments in Latin for scholars. Within weeks, printers turn them into German and sell copies in many towns. Tradespeople who have never met Luther are soon arguing about his ideas.
look.prompt: How did the printing press change what happened to Luther's ideas? What tool plays a similar role today?

check.q: What did Luther's 95 Theses criticize?
check.why: The 95 Theses criticized the sale of indulgences.

check.q: Why did the printing press matter to the Reformation?
check.why: Printers copied Luther's writings by the thousands, so his ideas spread fast.

check.q: What did Luther teach about how people are saved?
check.why: Luther taught that people are saved by God's grace through faith.

lessons.title: Many Churches, Three Families
lessons.mainIdea: After Luther came Calvin, other Protestant churches and a Catholic reform, leaving three large Christian families today.
reading: Other reformers followed Luther. John Calvin led the church in Geneva, Switzerland, from the 1540s. His ideas shaped Presbyterian and Reformed churches. In England, King Henry VIII broke with the pope in 1534, and the Church of England formed. Later came Baptists, Methodists and many more *denominations*, separate church groups.

The Catholic Church also reformed itself. The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563. It restated Catholic teaching and set new rules for training priests. New orders, such as the Jesuits, founded schools and sent missionaries around the world. The Reformation years also brought religious wars, and many people died.

Today, Christianity is often described in three large families. Catholics are the largest. Protestants include thousands of denominations. The Orthodox churches are strong in Eastern Europe, Greece and Russia. All three share the Bible, *baptism* and the belief that Jesus is the Christ, but they differ on leadership, worship and some beliefs.

words.d: a separate group or family of churches, such as Methodist or Baptist
the Christian rite of washing or immersing in water to welcome a person into the church

look.title: Three Christian Families
look.cite: Pew Research Center, Global Christianity, 2011 (estimates for 2010)
look.prompt: Which family is largest? About what fraction of all Christians is Catholic?

check.q: Which reformer led the church in Geneva?
check.why: John Calvin led the church in Geneva; his ideas shaped Presbyterian and Reformed churches.

check.q: What was the Council of Trent?
choices: A Catholic council that reformed and restated teaching
check.why: The Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) was part of the Catholic Church's own reform.

check.q: What is a denomination?
choices: A separate group or family of churches
A painted image of a saint
check.why: A denomination is a separate church group, such as Baptist or Methodist.

lessons.title: The Americas and the Black Church
lessons.mainIdea: Christianity came to the Americas with European colonizers, and enslaved Africans and their descendants built churches of their own.
reading: From 1492 on, Spanish, Portuguese and French explorers brought Catholic missionaries to the Americas. English settlers brought Protestant churches. Some missionaries defended Native peoples, but conquest and forced conversion caused great suffering. Many Native Americans today are Christian, and many also keep their own traditions.

Enslaved Africans were brought to the Americas by force. Many were taught a Christianity that told them to obey. They heard their own message in the Bible too, especially in the story of the Exodus. They sang *spirituals*, songs of faith and freedom, like Go Down, Moses. Some worshiped in secret gatherings.

Free Black Christians founded their own churches. In Philadelphia, Richard Allen led the founding of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, organized in 1816. The *Black church* became a center of worship, schooling and community life. It gave leaders and meeting places to the fight against slavery and, later, segregation.

words.d: a religious song created by enslaved Africans in America, often about faith and freedom
the churches founded and led by African Americans, central to worship and community life

look.title: One Story, Two Hearers
look.text: A slaveholder reads the Bible and chooses verses about servants obeying. An enslaved woman hears the same Bible and remembers Moses telling Pharaoh, let my people go. That night she sings about it in the fields.
look.prompt: How can two people read the same book so differently? Why might the Exodus story matter so much to enslaved people?

check.q: What are spirituals?
choices: Religious songs of faith and freedom created by enslaved Africans
check.why: Spirituals were songs of faith and freedom created by enslaved Africans in America.

check.q: Who led the founding of the African Methodist Episcopal Church?
check.why: Richard Allen led the founding of the AME Church, organized in Philadelphia in 1816.

check.q: Which Bible story spoke strongly to many enslaved people?
choices: The Exodus from slavery in Egypt
check.why: The Exodus tells of people freed from slavery, and spirituals like Go Down, Moses retell it.

lessons.title: Civil Rights and Chicago's Churches
lessons.mainIdea: Black churches helped lead the civil rights movement, and Chicago today holds churches of every Christian family.
reading: In the 1950s and 1960s, the *civil rights movement* worked to end segregation and win voting rights. Many of its meetings were held in Black churches. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist minister. In his Letter from Birmingham Jail, he quoted the prophets and pointed to Paul. He argued that unjust laws must be resisted peacefully.

Chicago has its own church history. Thomas Dorsey, called the father of gospel music, led a choir at Pilgrim Baptist Church on the South Side from the 1930s. *Gospel music* spread from Chicago churches across the country. King himself lived on Chicago's West Side in 1966 to protest unfair housing.

Today Chicago holds churches of every family. Holy Name Cathedral is the seat of the Catholic archbishop. There are Greek, Serbian and Ukrainian Orthodox churches. There are Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist and Pentecostal churches, and Mass in Spanish, Polish and many other languages. Many Chicagoans also belong to other faiths or to none.

words.d: the 1950s and 1960s struggle to end segregation and protect equal rights in the United States
a style of Christian music that grew in Black churches, with Chicago as a key center

look.title: From the Letter from Birmingham Jail
look.text: Injustice anywhere threatens justice everywhere. People everywhere are tied together, so what harms one community directly affects all of them.
look.cite: Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from Birmingham Jail, April 16, 1963; in our own words (the letter is under copyright)
look.prompt: King was answering people who said he was an outsider in Birmingham. How does this idea answer them?

check.q: Where were many civil rights meetings held?
check.why: Black churches were key meeting places for the civil rights movement.

check.q: Who is called the father of gospel music?
check.why: Thomas Dorsey, who led a choir at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago, is called the father of gospel music.

check.q: Why did King write the Letter from Birmingham Jail?
choices: To answer clergy who called the protests unwise
check.why: King wrote to answer local clergy who had called the protests unwise and untimely.

choices: Reformation, Nicaea, East-West split, Paul's letters
East-West split, Paul's letters, Nicaea, Reformation
Paul's letters, Nicaea, East-West split, Reformation
review.why: Paul wrote c. 50 to 60 CE, Nicaea met in 325, the split came in 1054, and the Reformation began in 1517.

review.q: Which belief do Christians share across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches?
choices: That the pope leads all churches
That only Latin may be used
review.why: All three families believe Jesus is the Christ, though they differ on leadership and worship.

review.q: What did Constantine's Edict of Milan change?
choices: It allowed Christians to worship freely
review.why: In 313 CE the Edict of Milan allowed Christians to worship freely.

review.q: How do the Catholic and Orthodox churches differ on leadership?
choices: Orthodox follow the pope; Catholics follow patriarchs
Catholics follow the pope; Orthodox churches are led by patriarchs and bishops
review.why: The pope leads the Catholic Church; the Orthodox churches are led by patriarchs and bishops.

review.q: Galatians 3:28 says there is neither Jew nor Greek. What is Paul teaching?
choices: That believers should split into groups
That the Temple should be rebuilt
That believers are one despite their differences
review.why: Paul tells a mixed group that differences should not divide them in Christ.

review.q: What did Luther teach was the highest authority?
review.why: Luther taught that the Bible was the highest authority for Christians.
Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead, and they celebrate this at Easter.

review.q: What role did the Black church play in American history?
choices: It was a center of worship, schooling and the struggle for freedom
review.why: The Black church gave worship, schooling and leadership to the fight against slavery and segregation.
